samples.summary: Vendored copy of mermaid's private `directiveRegex`/`frontMatterRegex` with no drift detection under a caret dependency range. `packages/notes/package.json:68` pins `mermaid: ^11.16.0`, so a routine minor/patch upgrade can change what the engine recognizes as a config carrier while these copies stay put; the file's own comment states that recognizing LESS than the engine is the whole failure mode. verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. packages/notes/src/view/mermaid.ts:177-188 declares DIRECTIVE_RE and FRONTMATTER_RE with a comment saying they are "copied verbatim from its `src/utils/regexes.ts` (`directiveRegex` / `frontMatterRegex`, mermaid 11.16.0)" and that "Recognizing LESS than the engine does is the whole failure mode here". packages/notes/package.json:68 declares `"mermaid": "^11.16.0"` — a caret range, no exact pin and no overrides/resolutions found. A repo-wide grep for stripConfigDirectives/DIRECTIVE_RE/directiveRegex/frontMatterRegex returns only mermaid.ts (177-205, 418) and docs/design/notes/notes.md:369,373 — there is no test exercising the strip and therefore no upstream-parity check that would fail on drift; the design doc records the reuse decision but imposes no pinning obligation. Refutation grounds considered and rejected: `already-guarded` fails because the file itself states `secure` (mermaid.ts:158-175) pins only TOP-LEVEL keys and sanitizeSvg (mermaid.ts:283-292) only rejects fetch-carrying CSS, so neither renders an under-recognizing strip harmless; `out-of-scope` fails because "Scope & approach fit … wrong layer/abstraction" is explicitly in this lens's lane and coupling the notes package to a non-exported upstream implementation detail is an approach-fit judgement, not a line-level logic bug.

finding.summary: Hand-rolled SVG sanitizer reinvents DOMPurify, which the same change already pulls into the dependency graph
finding.evidence: `sanitizeSvgMarkup()` (mermaid.ts:203-230) hand-rolls a *denylist* sanitizer (DROPPED_TAGS / URL_ATTRS / scrubCss regexes over `@import` and `url(...)`) for note-derived markup. mermaid@11.16.0 — added by this diff — already depends on dompurify@3.4.12 (pnpm-lock.yaml, `mermaid@11.16.0` snapshot lists `dompurify: 3.4.12`), the industry-standard, allowlist-based, actively-maintained sanitizer, and no repo module currently provides sanitization (grep for DOMPurify/sanitize* in packages/** hits only this new file). Reuse-over-reinvent is the repo norm; a bespoke regex/denylist pass over untrusted content is the kind of thing that should reuse the existing dependency instead of being re-implemented per feature, and a denylist is inherently weaker than the allowlist DOMPurify would apply. Reviewed as a reuse/approach-fit concern, not as a specific vulnerability (that is the security lens's call).

verdict.reason: The finding claims mermaid.ts hand-rolls a denylist SVG sanitizer (`sanitizeSvgMarkup()` with `DROPPED_TAGS`/`URL_ATTRS`/`scrubCss`) instead of reusing DOMPurify. None of those symbols exist anywhere in the repo (repo-wide grep: zero hits). The actual code does exactly what the reviewer prescribes: `loadPurifier()` (mermaid.ts:148-151) imports `dompurify`, `sanitizeSvg()` (mermaid.ts:283-292) calls `purify.sanitize(svg, PURIFY_CONFIG)`, and `PURIFY_CONFIG` (mermaid.ts:207-232) is allowlist-based via `USE_PROFILES: {svg, svgFilters, html}` with a narrowed `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP`; `FORBID_TAGS`/`FORBID_ATTR` are additive hardening on top of the allowlist, not a replacement. DOMPurify is a declared direct dependency at packages/notes/package.json:63, so the change explicitly adopts the existing library rather than reinventing it. The only regex work (`CSS_EXTERNAL_RE`/`isSafeCss`, mermaid.ts:238-265) runs after DOMPurify on `<style>` text and `style` attributes — CSS content DOMPurify does not parse — and makes no tag/attribute allow-deny decisions, so it is a narrow supplement, not a duplicated sanitizer module. The reuse/approach-fit premise therefore has no basis in this working tree.
